policy.purpose: Evidence ledger for canonical Pattern Dictionary Wave 4 before any runtime publication.
policy.runtime_lock: data/patterns.json remains canonical 60 throughout this source-verification gate.
policy.primary_palette_rule: A fixed primary palette is an editorial recognition reference unless a source establishes color as identity-relevant. It is never presented as the only valid colorway.
policy.relationship_rule: similar and often_confused_with are visual-discovery relationships, not claims of shared historical origin unless explicitly sourced.
policy.qualification_rule: Use qualified when the term is fundamentally a technique, textile effect, historical decorative style, textile tradition, or other broad family that does not resolve to one uniquely fixed motif.

patterns.term_scope: Baroque running-scroll ornamental family rather than one uniquely fixed repeat

verified_names.ja: バロック・スクロール

ja: バロック調スクロール

patterns.structure: Running foliate scrolls repeat or extend through a field, often using acanthus-derived foliage and curved stems; exact scroll shape, density, and symmetry vary across Baroque ornament.

color_guidance.reason: Scroll structure and historical ornamental treatment carry recognition; no fixed Baroque palette defines the family.

patterns.qualification: Baroque is a historical decorative style, and running scrolls were a widespread form of Baroque floral ornament rather than one universal pattern. Pattern Dictionary therefore treats Baroque Scroll as a qualified discovery family built around running foliate scrollwork.

supports: running scroll as a widespread form of Baroque floral decoration

patterns.term_scope: European decorative style adapting imagined or interpreted East Asian motifs, not one fixed motif
patterns.structure: Decorative compositions combine varied motifs such as pagodas, pavilions, figures, flowering plants, birds, landscapes, and other East Asian-inspired imagery; layouts range from scenic panels to repeated surface decoration.

color_guidance.reason: Chinoiserie is identified by its decorative vocabulary and historical styling rather than a fixed color scheme.

patterns.qualification: Chinoiserie is a broad European decorative style that adapted and reimagined East Asian motifs across many media. It does not resolve to one canonical repeat or one stable motif inventory, so the reference image must be explicitly representative.

supports: chinoiserie as a European decorative style
varied recurring motif vocabulary rather than one fixed pattern
Chinese figures, pagodas, landscapes, birds and flowering plants as varied elements

patterns.term_scope: Bargello or flame-stitch counted-thread embroidery technique and its characteristic stepped zigzag visual

ja: フロレンティン・ステッチ

patterns.structure: Rows of vertical stitches step up and down in counted increments, producing regular peaks and valleys or sharper flame-like zigzags; different step sequences can produce multiple Bargello motifs.

color_guidance.reason: The stepped stitch geometry identifies the visual; vivid gradients are common recognition cues but are not definitional.

patterns.qualification: Flame stitch is closely tied to Bargello counted-thread embroidery and describes a technique/visual construction rather than one universal printed repeat. Pattern Dictionary represents the characteristic stepped peaks and valleys without claiming a canonical stitch count or color sequence.

supports: flame stitch as a name for Bargello work
vertical stitches stepped to create regular peaks and valleys

patterns.term_scope: named tree-centered symbolic motif with many historical variants

ja: ツリー・オブ・ライフ

patterns.structure: A prominent stylized tree forms the central motif, often with branching foliage, flowers, fruit, birds, or animals arranged around or flanking it; details vary by period and culture.

color_guidance.reason: Recognition comes from the central branching tree composition; colors and accompanying fauna vary widely.

supports: animals flanking a tree as a long-standing composition
fruit-bearing tree and wildlife pattern usage

patterns.term_scope: watered or rippled textile surface effect rather than one fixed motif
patterns.structure: Undulating, rippled, woodgrain-like or watered bands appear across the textile surface through finishing, pressure, weave interaction, or related processes; exact wave geometry is inherently variable.

color_guidance.reason: The shifting watered surface effect is the identifying cue; moiré occurs in many colors and fibers.

patterns.qualification: Moiré denotes a watered textile surface effect produced by several methods, not one fixed printed motif. The reference image therefore represents characteristic rippled bands without implying a universal wave layout.

supports: moiré as several methods affecting a fabric surface

sources.publisher: National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution

patterns.term_scope: named Japanese arrow-feather or arrow design
patterns.structure: Repeated arrow or arrow-feather forms align in rows, commonly as pointed chevrons or paired feather shapes that can alternate direction.

color_guidance.reason: Arrow-feather geometry carries recognition; palette varies across textiles.

supports: rows of large and small arrows

patterns.term_scope: named continuous interlocking fret pattern
patterns.structure: Interlocking angular manji-derived fret lines tessellate continuously, creating a repeated rectilinear field of hooked and H-like forms.

color_guidance.reason: The continuous angular fret construction defines the pattern; color is variable.

supports: common Japanese dress use in the Edo period

patterns.term_scope: named Japanese scale pattern based on repeated triangles
patterns.structure: Triangles repeat edge-to-edge as a geometric field, traditionally read as stylized scales; regular equilateral or near-equilateral triangular units are a common formulation.

color_guidance.reason: Repeated triangular scale geometry identifies the motif; historical uses span many palettes.

sources.publisher: Agency for Cultural Affairs, Japan — Cultural Heritage Online

patterns.term_scope: named Japanese vertically rising paired-curve pattern
patterns.structure: Paired curving lines swell and narrow repeatedly as they rise vertically, creating hourglass or gourd-like compartments that may contain secondary motifs.

color_guidance.reason: The vertically repeated swelling curves carry recognition; inserted motifs and colors vary.

sources.publisher: Agency for Cultural Affairs, Japan — Cultural Heritage Online
supports: continuous curves forming vertically repeated gourd-like shapes
named variants based on inserted motifs

patterns.term_scope: named Japanese basket-weave-derived lattice pattern
patterns.structure: Diagonal strips or lines interlace into a repeating basket-derived lattice of triangular and hexagonal openings, commonly read as the geometry of woven bamboo.

color_guidance.reason: The interlaced basket lattice defines the motif; natural basket colors are only illustrative.

patterns.term_scope: kanoko spotted visual convention closely tied to kanoko shibori resist-dye technique
patterns.structure: Many small tied or resist-dyed spots repeat across the cloth; a common kanoko unit reads as a small undyed square or spot with a tiny center mark, but scale and arrangement vary with technique and design.

color_guidance.reason: The dense resist-spotted visual is the recognition cue; the technique appears in many colorways.

patterns.qualification: Kanoko is inseparable from kanoko shibori in many historical textiles: the dotted visual is produced by a resist-dye process and does not define one universal repeat. Pattern Dictionary therefore separates the recognizable spotted visual convention from the broader dyeing technique.

supports: kanoko as a popular shibori variation
typical small square with center dot

patterns.term_scope: named Japanese floral-lozenge motif
patterns.structure: A stylized flower is organized within a diamond or lozenge outline, repeated singly or as a field; petal treatment can vary while the floral-lozenge identity remains.

color_guidance.reason: The floral lozenge construction defines the motif; color is not intrinsic.

patterns.term_scope: same or sharkskin fine-dot komon visual produced within a fine-pattern dyeing tradition
patterns.structure: Extremely fine dots form repeated overlapping or arcing semicircular units, producing a sharkskin-like field that can read as nearly solid from a distance.

color_guidance.reason: Minute dotted arc structure defines the visual; Edo/Tokyo komon is produced in many colors.

patterns.qualification: Same Komon is a named fine-dot pattern, but it is also embedded in the stencil-dyed komon technique and craft tradition. Pattern Dictionary therefore qualifies the entry so the dotted sharkskin visual is not confused with all Edo/Tokyo Some-Komon or with one fixed stencil density.

sources.publisher: Bureau of Industrial and Labor Affairs, Tokyo Metropolitan Government
supports: Tokyo Some-Komon as repeated minute-pattern dyeing
gokuzame/fine sharkskin as a representative pattern

sources.publisher: University of Michigan Museum of Art

patterns.term_scope: named Japanese motif pairing plovers with waves
patterns.structure: Small stylized plovers fly above, beside, or through repeated wave forms; exact bird count and wave rendering vary while the wave-plus-plover pairing remains the motif.

color_guidance.reason: The pairing of plovers and waves is the identifying cue; palette varies by medium.

supports: 波千鳥 / plovers and waves motif terminology
chidori terminology and Japanese cultural context

patterns.term_scope: named Japanese comma-shaped tomoe motif
patterns.structure: One or more rounded comma-like forms curve around a common center or repeat across a field; single, double, and triple arrangements exist.

color_guidance.reason: The curved comma form carries recognition; historical and modern examples use many palettes.

supports: association with crests and samurai culture

patterns.term_scope: family of Japanese resist-dye techniques producing many different patterns
patterns.structure: Fabric is folded, stitched, bound, sheathed, knotted, twisted, compressed, or otherwise resisted before dyeing, producing varied rings, spots, lines, grids, and pictorial compositions depending on method.

color_guidance.reason: Indigo-and-white is a strong recognition convention, but shibori technique is not color-defined.

patterns.qualification: Shibori is a family of resist-dye techniques, not one pattern. Any reference image is necessarily representative of one shibori visual outcome and must not be presented as canonical for the entire tradition.

supports: folding, stitching, binding, sheathing and knotting as resist methods
shibori as a specialized textile-art field
Kyoto Kanoko Shibori as one refined technique within the broader practice

patterns.term_scope: wax-resist dyeing textile tradition with a wide diversity of patterns
patterns.structure: Hot wax is applied as resist in dots, lines, or drawn/printed areas before dyeing; repeated waxing and dyeing can build geometric, floral, figurative, or symbolic patterns.

color_guidance.reason: Traditional palettes vary by region and practice; wax-resist construction is more fundamental than any color pair.

patterns.qualification: Batik is a wax-resist dyeing technique and living textile tradition with a wide diversity of regional patterns and symbols. It is not one fixed repeat, so the reference image is representative only.

supports: Indonesian Batik as techniques, symbolism and culture
wide diversity of patterns and influences

patterns.term_scope: South Asian tie-resist textile technique and tradition characterized by numerous tied points
patterns.structure: Small points of cloth are tightly tied before dyeing, creating many resist dots that can be arranged into geometric, figurative, clustered, border, or field patterns; related tying methods produce different named outcomes.

color_guidance.reason: Bright contrasting colors are common recognition cues, but tying method and dotted resist structure define the craft more than palette.

patterns.qualification: Bandhani is a tie-resist technique and textile tradition capable of producing many named layouts, not one universal dotted repeat. Pattern Dictionary uses a characteristic dotted resist field as a representative visual only.

sources.publisher: Government of Rajasthan — Handmade in Rajasthan
supports: multiple named patterns depending on tying method

sources.publisher: Government of Rajasthan — Handmade in Rajasthan
supports: variety of patterns from different tying methods

patterns.term_scope: Kachchh/Sindh-linked resist and block-print textile tradition with complex geometric pattern vocabularies
patterns.structure: Precisely registered block-printed repeats commonly combine geometric stars, medallions, grids, borders, and floral elements through repeated resist, mordant, dye, wash, and drying stages.

color_guidance.reason: Government of Kachchh describes Ajrakh geometry across indigo, madder, black, and white, while individual textiles still vary.

patterns.qualification: Ajrakh is a textile-printing tradition and process, not one fixed motif. Its recognizable geometric vocabulary and common dye family can guide discovery, but no single star, medallion, grid, or layout is canonical for all Ajrakh.

supports: indigo, madder, black and white palette
multi-stage washing, dyeing, printing and drying process
Ajrakh as hand block printing tradition in Kutch
multiple blocks and varied textile uses

patterns.term_scope: Indian painted, mordant-dyed and resist-dyed textile process/tradition rather than one fixed pattern
patterns.structure: Designs are built through multistep drawing, mordant application, resist, dye baths, and hand painting or related block-print processes, supporting floral, figurative, narrative, and geometric compositions.

color_guidance.reason: Historic kalamkari uses characteristic natural-dye families, but technique and regional practice are broader than one palette.

patterns.qualification: Kalamkari names a textile-making process and regional tradition spanning hand-painted and related printed works with many compositions. It is not one universal motif, so the reference image must be presented as representative rather than canonical.

supports: multistep mordant, wax-resist and dye process
process used to create varied designs
regional production of many textile types

supports: Srikalahasti Kalamkari as hand-painted or block-printed cotton textile craft
